questions.question: Ravi builds a solid cube out of centimetre cubes. It is 3 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 3 cubes tall. Walking all the way around it he can count 26 cubes on the outside, and exactly 1 cube is buried in the middle where nobody can see it. What is the volume of Ravi's cube?
questions.explain: Volume counts every unit cube that fills the space, hidden ones included: 3 layers of 9 cubes is 27 cm³. The usual trap is answering 26, the number you can see, and forgetting the cube buried inside.

questions.question: Nadia builds a solid cube of centimetre cubes that is 4 cubes long, 4 cubes wide and 4 cubes tall. Each flat layer holds 16 cubes, and the cube is 4 layers tall. Some cubes sit deep in the middle where they cannot be seen from any side. What is the volume of Nadia's cube?
questions.explain: Volume is the number of cubes in one layer times the number of layers: 16 × 4 = 64 cm³. Answering 56 means counting only the cubes showing on the outside and missing the 8 cubes hidden in the core.

questions.question: Sofia builds a solid block from centimetre cubes. It is 4 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 2 cubes tall. Looking down from above she sees only the top layer of 12 cubes, because a second layer of 12 cubes is hidden underneath it. What is the volume of her block?
questions.explain: Two layers of 12 cubes make 24 cm³ — the hidden bottom layer takes up just as much space as the top one. The common slip is reporting 12, only the cubes in sight.

questions.question: Leo builds a solid cube of centimetre cubes that is 5 cubes long, 5 cubes wide and 5 cubes tall, so it is made of 125 cubes in all. Every cube touching an outside face can be seen. The cubes that are left over form a smaller solid cube, 3 cubes long, 3 wide and 3 tall, deep inside. How many of Leo's cubes are completely hidden?
questions.explain: The hidden part is itself a cube 3 by 3 by 3, so 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubes are buried where you cannot see them. Saying none are hidden, or giving 98, describes the cubes on the outside instead.

questions.question: A solid prism is built from centimetre cubes as 3 identical layers stacked on top of each other, and each layer is 4 cubes by 5 cubes. From where Mei stands she can see only the top layer and part of one side. What is the volume of the whole prism?
questions.explain: One layer is 4 × 5 = 20 cubes and there are 3 layers, so 20 × 3 = 60 cm³. Answering 40 comes from counting only the layers in sight and dropping the hidden one.

questions.question: Which of these always gives the volume of a solid rectangular prism built from centimetre cubes, counting the hidden cubes too?
options: Count every cube you can see from the outside and stop there
Multiply the number of cubes in one layer by the number of layers
Count the small squares showing on all six faces
Add the length, the width and the height together
questions.explain: Every layer holds the same number of cubes, so layer size times number of layers also reaches the cubes buried inside. Counting only what shows leaves out the middle, and counting face squares measures surface area, not volume.

questions.question: Owen glues centimetre cubes together into a solid model of a cereal box that is 6 cubes long, 4 cubes wide and 5 cubes tall. What is the volume of his model?
questions.explain: Each layer is 6 × 4 = 24 cubes and the model is 5 layers tall, so 24 × 5 = 120 cm³. Getting 96 means only 4 layers were counted, forgetting a layer hidden under the others.

questions.question: A solid prism made of centimetre cubes has a volume of 48 cm³. Each layer of the prism holds 12 cubes. How many layers tall is the prism?
questions.explain: Since every layer holds 12 cubes, 48 ÷ 12 = 4 layers. Answering 3 usually comes from counting only the layers you can spot from outside instead of working from the total number of cubes.

questions.question: Jayden looks at a solid cube built from centimetre cubes that is 3 cubes long, 3 cubes wide and 3 cubes tall. He carefully counts every cube he can see from the outside, gets 26, and says the volume is 26 cm³. What should his teacher tell him?
options: He missed the 1 cube hidden in the middle, so the volume is 27 cm³.
He should count the squares on the six faces instead, giving 54 cm³.
He is right, because volume means the cubes you can see.
He should add 3 + 3 + 3, so the volume is 9 cm³.
questions.explain: Volume counts all the cubes that fill the space, so the buried cube counts too: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cm³. Counting only visible cubes always leaves the middle of a solid out.

questions.question: Liam fills a rectangular bin at school completely with centimetre cubes. The bottom layer holds 200 cubes and the bin is 10 layers deep. Standing above it he can see only the top 2 layers, so he writes 400 cm³. Knowing that 1000 cm³ of space holds 1 litre, what is the real capacity of the bin?
questions.explain: All 10 layers count, even the ones hidden below: 200 × 10 = 2000 cm³, and 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2 litres. Using only the 2 layers in sight gives 400 cm³, and dividing by the wrong number breaks the 1000 cm³ = 1 litre link.

questions.question: Priya builds a solid cube of centimetre cubes that is 4 long, 4 wide and 4 tall, then paints the whole outside. She counts 56 painted cubes on the outside of the finished cube. Which statement about her cube is correct?
options: Nothing is hidden, so the volume is 56 cm³.
8 cubes are hidden inside, but the volume is still 56 cm³.
8 cubes are hidden inside with no paint, so the volume is 64 cm³.
16 cubes are hidden inside, so the volume is 72 cm³.
questions.explain: The whole cube is 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³, and the unpainted cubes form a small 2 by 2 by 2 block, since 64 − 56 = 8. The trap is letting the 56 cubes you can see stand in for the volume.

questions.question: Ava is packing a small gift box with centimetre cubes. The box holds 5 cubes along the front, 3 cubes across, and 4 cubes up to the top. She has already laid 1 full layer of cubes on the bottom. How many more cubes does she need to fill the box completely?
questions.explain: Each layer is 5 × 3 = 15 cubes and the box is 4 layers deep, so it holds 60 cubes; with 1 layer already packed, 60 − 15 = 45 more are needed. Counting only the layers you can see down into, or forgetting the layer already in the box, gives too few.
